title: Telemedicine and Triage
answer: Symptom routing, camera-based vital signs, wearables, conversational care and mental health signals.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Symptom Triage and Routing
children.blurb: Symptom triage and routing uses AI to assess patient-reported symptoms, estimate urgency, and direct patients to appropriate care settings such as self-care, primary care, urgent care, or emergency services.

children.name: Vital Signs from a Camera
children.blurb: Vital signs from a camera refers to software that estimates physiological measurements such as heart rate, respiratory rate, and sometimes blood oxygen saturation from a standard video feed of a person's face or upper body.

children.name: Wearable Data in Clinical Care
children.blurb: Wearable data in clinical care covers continuous or intermittent physiological signals collected outside the clinic, such as heart rate, activity, sleep, blood oxygen, glucose, and single-lead electrocardiogram readings, and their use in remote monitoring, triage, and chronic disease management.

children.name: Conversational Care and Its Limits
children.blurb: Conversational care refers to AI systems that interact with patients through text or voice to collect symptoms, answer questions, and support triage before or instead of a human clinician.

children.name: Digital Signals of Mental Health
children.blurb: Digital signals of mental health are behavioral and physiological data collected through phones, wearables, and telehealth platforms that may indicate changes in mood, sleep, activity, speech, or social engagement.

sections.body: Telemedicine and triage covers the ways artificial intelligence tries to move parts of a medical visit outside the clinic. Symptom routing tools ask a patient a series of questions and suggest whether to seek urgent care, see a doctor, or stay home. Camera-based vital signs use video of a face to estimate pulse and breathing rate without contact. Wearables collect heart rate, sleep, activity, and sometimes oxygen saturation over days or weeks. Conversational care uses text or voice agents for intake, follow-up questions, and structured mental health exercises. Digital signals of mental health look at patterns in speech, typing, and phone use for possible mood changes.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Symptom triage is reasonably good at common, low-risk complaints but still misses serious conditions and often sends people to care they do not need. Camera vital signs work only under good lighting and with a still, well-lit face, and they are not accurate enough for clinical decisions. Wearable data is abundant but noisy, and most clinics do not yet act on it in real time. Conversational care handles scripted tasks well but cannot manage open-ended distress or reliably detect emergencies. Mental health signal research is mostly exploratory and not validated for diagnosis. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows both the scale of activity and the real risk of harm.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section move from the first point of contact to longer-term monitoring. Symptom Triage and Routing explains how a patient is sorted by urgency and where the sorting goes wrong. Vital Signs from a Camera covers the specific technique of measuring pulse and breathing from video and its practical limits. Wearable Data in Clinical Care looks at what continuous device data adds to a visit and why it is hard to use. Conversational Care and Its Limits examines what text and voice agents can do in structured care and where they stop. Digital Signals of Mental Health reviews the passive sensing research that tries to infer mood from everyday phone use, and why that remains uncertain.
